Thank you, Madam Chair. Good morning, my name is Angela Gardner, General Manager Utilities and Environment. This first report is the Climate Action Strategy Community Engagement Report, and it provides an overview of engagement activities undertaken in 2024 and 2025 to inform the development of Saskatoon's new climate action strategy, which will replace the existing low emissions community plan and adaptation strategy that was presented to Council in 2019.
I would like to introduce Amber Weckworth, our Climate Manager within the Sustainability Department to provide a presentation this morning.

Good morning and thank you for the introduction. I am pleased to be bringing you this report, which summarizes the community engagement that's supported, that's supporting the development of the 4th Climate Action Strategy, which will be coming forward for approval later in 2026.

Next slide, please. Since 2015, Saskatoon has been committed to climate action through the global covenant of mayors. The low emissions community plan and a corporate climate adaptation strategy were approved in 2019.

In 2023, Council adopted an updated greenhouse gas reduction target of net 0 by 2050 and noted that a plan that considered the impact of climate change to the community still remained outstanding at that time.
Now, in 2026, we plan to bring forward an updated climate action strategy, and we're starting with this engagement summary. Next slide, please.

The updated climate action strategy will replace the existing low emissions community plan and the corporate climate adaptation strategy. It will present a comprehensive approach for climate readiness.
The presents measures that reduce carbon pollution with efforts to prepare the city and the community for the impacts of the changing climate.
It will also embed equity, reconciliation, prosperity, and meopomotsuin, or the good life throughout all the actions. Next slide, please.

Community engagement on the Climate Action Strategy has occurred throughout 2024 and 2025. We have engaged with the public, subject matter experts, targeted stakeholders, and city staff to help inform the climate action strategy.

Some of our key milestones included, in summer 2024, our team met with individual stakeholders and community groups working directly with vulnerable populations as they have an important role as we look at building community resilience.
Then, in spring 2025, we held a workshop with a broader set of stakeholder organizations to further explore the impacts of climate change in Saskatoon and some possible actions to repair.
Throughout the summer and into the fall of 2025, we had an online public survey which covered both carbon reduction and resilience actions. It was available to the general public.
Then last fall, we held information sessions with a broad spectrum of organizations, businesses, and associations in Saskatoon together feedback on proposed carbon reduction actions.

An Indigenous perspective was heard through meetings with a representative from the Indigenous Technical Advisory Committee, participation by Indigenous organizations in events, and in the survey, participation at the FSIN Indigenous Sustainability Summit, and meetings with Indigenous Relations staff within the city of Saskatoon.

Then to bring up business perspective, numerous businesses and business organizations, namely the business improvement districts, the NSPA and SREEDA were heard from through events, the surveys, and meetings.
These organizations all share also shared engagement information with their members.
The engagement results were then published on May 26, and all who participated in the engagement were notified to provide them an additional week to review and digest the results.
A similar approach will be used for the final climate action strategy. Next slide, please.
Throughout these engagement events, we heard that community members are concerned about the expected impacts of a changing climate in Saskatoon, with an average rating of 4 out of 5 in the survey.
In fact, many described impacts occurring already today, not in the future, such as wildfire smoke that impacts their daily lives.
When asked why climate action matters, participants stated that it's about protecting future generations, their health and safety, and the opportunity to build a better city.

Next slide, please. Many also stress that individual action alone is not enough. Most participants, about 87%, either agreed or somewhat agreed that institutions and businesses should be leading climate action instead of just individuals.

Next slide. For carbon reduction, sometimes referred to as climate mitigation, which is about reducing our greenhouse gas emissions or carbon pollution by reducing electricity gas or other fuels or producing less landfill emissions.
For carbon reduction, we heard that actions that address high emissions sources such as building energy, use, and those that have other benefits like improving equity or safety should be prioritized.
We also heard concern about shifting the cost of burden, cost or burden of climate impacts onto those least able to handle them, such as low income individuals or small businesses.
The report includes more details with specific feedback on individual topic areas and actions. Next slide, please.
So for climate resilience, which we sometimes refer to as climate adaptation, which is about preparing our organization and the community to manage the impacts of a warming climate.
On climate resilience, we consistently heard that the impacts of climate change are unevenly distributed.

As such, participants prioritize actions that reduce harm, such as prioritizing vulnerable populations, strength and essential services and utilities, and build resilience into our housing, infrastructure and public spaces to ensure they are designed for future climate conditions.
Again, the full report outlines all the specific feedback on individual risks and actions. Next slide, please.
The full climate action strategy is expected to come to Council for approval in August. It will outline actions to reduce carbon and improve climate resilience in Saskatoon.
The new strategy will supersede the LEC plan and corporate climate action adaptation strategy.
If the strategy is approved, the administration would use the climate action strategy as a high level framework for work planning and budget requests to meet our climate targets and goals.
Each action will require further budget approval from City Council and further engagement before being designed and implemented.

This next report provides an update on Saskatoon's flood control strategy and seeks approval
to proceed with the 9th and final project within the first phase of the program.
The strategy was originally approved in 2018.
It was a 9 year 54 million dollar initiative aimed at reducing flooding in 10 high priority areas across the city.
The proposed project at 463 and 1st Avenue North is based on a completed feasibility assessment,
which confirms that the project is technically viable and will reduce flood risk for nearby properties during intense storm events.
The project includes constructing a large diameter storm sewer connection at the RCAF Memorial storm pond,
and improving the system's capacity to manage storm water in an area with a history of frequent flooding.
The report also highlights that this location ranked amongst the city's higher risk flood areas,
and that the project has been evaluated through a cost benefit analysis to maximize flood protection.
In addition to the storm sewer construction, the project will include dreading of the storm pond to restore its original storage capacity.
Subject to Council approval detailed design and tendering are planned for 2026 and 2027 with construction anticipated next summer.
Completion of this project will mark the inclusion of the first phase of the flood control strategy program.
We acknowledge that while this program has provided solutions to the top 10 high-risk areas,
there still remains other areas that may need to be addressed.
With that in mind, we intend to report back this fall with options for the next phase of the program.

related to urban forestry, climate resilience, and equity.
It will evaluate tree species and management practices suited to Saskatchewan's typically dry climate,
quantifying environmental benefits such as cooling and stormwater management,
and strengthen our ability to monitor canopy change and guide long-term planning decisions.
This project also includes a strong community engagement component to better understand how residents experience
and benefit from green infrastructure.

Good morning. Chair and committee members. My name is Doug Wigren, Saskatoon Fire Chief for the Saskatoon Fire Department.
With me today is Director of EMO, Pam Goldham Cloud, Acting Director for Community Relationships, Ryan Bradley, and Deputy Chief of Operations and Emergency Communications, Sean Foody.
This year in review report presentation provides committee with a high level overview of Saskatoon Fire Department's 2025 activities, pressures, and service priorities.
In 2025, the Department continued its delivery of emergency response, fire prevention, emergency communications, and community support services.
While operating in a complex environment marked by rising coal volumes, evolving social challenges and significant large scale emergency coordination requirements. Next slide, please.
The SFD responded to 28,719 calls for service, a 13.2% increase over 2024. Overdosed responses rose to 2,512, nearly double the previous year, and occurred across every Saskatoon neighborhood.

Encomment responses also continued to grow with 1,859 encampments, attended, and 116 encampment fires, reflecting the heightened risks associated with homelessness, addictions, and end adequate shelter.
This growing public safety issue has created competing priority demands which have contributed to backlogs in annual fire inspections.
In addition, the City's Emergency Operations Center was activated through EMO to support the northern wildfire evacuations.
Saskatoon hosted approximately 8,000 evacuees representing half of the 16,000 people displaced from northern Saskatchewan.
These pressures affected frontline operations and required support from all divisions across the SFD.
Despite these pressures, the Saskatoon Fire Department advanced several important initiatives to strengthen service delivery and long-term readiness. Next slide, please.

We developed and introduced a new mission statement, which is serving Saskatoon with exceptional fire and emergency response by champion collaboration and innovation for safety and risk reduction to build community resilience and a new vision statement to give you our best every day.

The mission and vision statements matter because they communicate to the public what the SFD stands for and these statements are guiding motivation for daily efforts and initiatives to serve Saskatoon. Next slide, please.
The SFD launched next year in 911, relocated its dispatch center and new CAD system. The system went live in February of 2026, completed a three-plus year long project.

We also enhanced our firefighter development through delivering live fire training at a regional training facility. This training is critical to support firefighter skills and understanding of the fire environment based on new building designs and lightweight construction materials.

Also, council's prior approval of constructions of fire stations 10 and 11. Also, position the SFD to better meet future growth and our challenge response times resulting from urban sprawl and population increase.

Our community relations team continues to support Saskatoon by working through with schools, community groups and with the elderly to promote fire safety emergency preparedness and awareness of the roles fire firefighters playing the community.
I note here we have just completed our 12th year of fire today program with 12 or sorry 15 high school students graduating from the eight week program this Thursday.
The fire cadet program has been very important to the SFD as Anna has supported us by producing three current SFD firefighters and three by law inspectors.

The fire community support program completed its first year and a half of operations at the end of 2025. The FCS team provides proactive support to transit and business improvement districts focusing on supporting individuals in need while maintaining a visual uniform presence to enhance safety for all.

In 2025, FCS responded to 3,308 incidents and completed 2003 and 2010 bus rides. Overall, the year review demonstrates the SFD's commitment to respond to an increasing to increasing community needs while continuing to invest in service capacity operational effectiveness and public safety.
